Pending tests (genetic testing, liver US, MRI) are confirmatory or staging tools—not required for diagnosis in this setting per established criteria (e.g., Pei et al. 2009): in patients >40 years, ≥2 cysts in each kidney on ultrasound is 100% sensitive for ADPKD; even in younger adults (30–39), ≥2 cysts per kidney has >95% sensitivity if there’s a positive family history — and here, the *clinical burden* (hypertension, declining eGFR, pain, infections) strongly supports disease expression regardless of family history. No contradictory findings (e.g., solid masses, complex Bosniak III/IV cysts, rapid growth, hemorrhage, enhancement) are reported — all described cysts are “anechoic”, i.e., simple. Thus, ADPKD is not just *likely* — it is the single most probable and best-explained diagnosis.

- Bilateral renal enlargement with multiple parenchymal anechoic (simple) cysts on ultrasound  
- Elevated serum creatinine (1.4 mg/dL) and BUN (29 mg/dL), indicating reduced kidney function

- No hematuria outside UTIs — argues against glomerulonephritis, stones, or malignancy
